notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Genesis 7, drawing on the sources I could access:

---

## Genesis 7 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### v. 1 — "Then the LORD said to Noah, 'Go into the ark…'"

**The Divine Invitation.** The Hebrew verb can be translated either "go" or "come" (KJV, ASV, NET have "Come"). Spurgeon made much of "Come," saying it implies God was already in the ark waiting to receive Noah: "The distinctive word of the gospel is a drawing word: 'Come.'" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-7-commentary) Ellicott likewise notes the task of building is over and after a week of collecting animals, Noah is to take up residence. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/7.htm)

**"I have found you righteous."** The Pulpit Commentary explains that "righteous before me" (literally "before my face") is "the usual Scriptural phrase for justification" (cf. Psalm 143:2), announcing Noah's justification in God's sight, not mere moral improvement. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm) Precept Austin adds that this is positional righteousness by grace through faith, citing Hebrews 11:7: Noah "became an heir of the righteousness which is according to faith." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-7-commentary)

**"In this generation."** The Pulpit Commentary notes this indicates the sphere of Noah's godly life and its exceptional character — "involving an opposing sentence of condemnation against his contemporaries" (Lange). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm)

**Family inclusion.** Precept Austin quotes Jon Courson on a "dynamic" (not a doctrine): the father's faith creates a place of salvation for his household, just as the Philippian jailer was told, "Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household" (Acts 16:31). Each person must still exercise personal faith. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-7-commentary)

---

### v. 2 — "seven pairs of every kind of clean animal … a pair of every kind of unclean animal"

**Clean/unclean distinction known before Moses.** Ellicott says there can be no reference to the Levitical law; rather the clean beasts were "such as from the days of Adam and Abel had been offered in sacrifice" — oxen, sheep, goats. Unclean would be camels, horses, asses, and animals not used for sacrifice. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/7.htm) The Pulpit Commentary agrees: the distinction was "of Divine institution, with reference to the necessities of sacrifice" (Genesis 8:20). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm) Utley (bible.org) notes this is in "a pre-Mosaic sacrificial setting." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/genesis-7.html)

**"Seven pairs" or "seven individuals"?** The Hebrew is literally "seven seven." The Pulpit Commentary lists both views: "seven pairs" (Vulgate, LXX, Murphy, Alford, Wordsworth) or "seven individuals" (Chrysostom, Augustine, Calvin, Keil, Delitzsch, Lange). The phrase "the male and his female" favors the pairs interpretation. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm) Ellicott leans toward seven individuals of each kind. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/7.htm) The NET Bible notes simply say "Or 'seven pairs' (cf. NRSV)." (https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/gen7_notes.htm)

---

### v. 3 — "seven pairs of every kind of bird"

**Clean birds implied.** The Pulpit Commentary notes that "clean" fowls are "left to be understood out of the foregoing verse." The Samaritan, Syriac, and LXX insert "clean" and also add a clause about unclean birds "manifestly to make the verse resemble the preceding." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm)

**Purpose: "to preserve their offspring."** The Pulpit Commentary renders it "to keep seed alive upon the face of all the earth." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm)

---

### v. 4 — "seven days from now I will send rain … forty days and forty nights"

**Seven days' warning.** The Pulpit Commentary says this gave Noah time to complete preparations and the world "one more opportunity to repent," noting Peele's suggestion that many may have repented, "though their bodies were drowned for their former impenitency." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm) Jewish tradition, noted by Ellicott, held these seven days were the mourning period for Methuselah, who died in the year of the flood. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/7.htm)

**The number 40.** Enduring Word lists the many biblical associations: Moses on Sinai (40 days), Israel's spies in Canaan (40 days), Israel in the wilderness (40 years), Elijah's journey (40 days), Jesus' temptation (40 days) — all periods of testing and purification. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-7/) The Pulpit Commentary likewise calls 40 "symbolical of a period of trial, ending in victory to the good and in ruin to the evil." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm)

**"Every living thing I have made."** The Hebrew word is *yekum*, meaning "whatever stands erect." Ellicott says it means not merely man and beast but "the whole existent state of things." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/7.htm)

---

### v. 5 — "Noah did all that the LORD had commanded him"

Both Enduring Word and Precept Austin treat this as a summary of Noah's complete obedience. The Pulpit Commentary draws attention to the name *Jehovah* used here (the God of salvation who interposed for Noah's safety), contrasted with *Elohim* in Genesis 6:22 (God in relation to all flesh). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm)

---

### v. 6 — "Noah was 600 years old"

The Pulpit Commentary notes the number six "is generally a Scriptural symbol of suffering. Christ suffered on the sixth day. In the Apocalypse the sixth seal, the sixth trumpet, the sixth vial introduce critical periods of affliction" (Wordsworth). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm) Ellicott calculates that Shem was about 100 years old and his brothers younger; all were married but apparently childless (cf. Genesis 11:10). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/7.htm)

---

### vv. 7–9 — Entering the ark; the animals came "two by two"

**Eight persons.** The Pulpit Commentary notes each son had only one wife: "polygamy, as it began among the Cainites, was most probably confined to them" (Poole). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm)

**Animals came by divine impulse.** Enduring Word, citing Spurgeon, says, "This largest and most complete menagerie that was ever gathered together was not collected by human skill; divine power alone could have accomplished such a task as that." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-7/) Precept Austin adds: "In obeying God others obey us. … When we are under authority, we can say 'Go,' 'Come,' 'Do this.' All things serve the man who serves the Divine Master, Christ." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-7-commentary)

**The seeming inconsistency** (clean by sevens in v.2, but "two by two" in vv.8–9) is resolved, per the Pulpit Commentary, by connecting vv.7–8 rather than vv.8–9, starting a new sentence at v.9. The LXX begins v.8 with "and." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm)

---

### v. 10 — "after seven days the floodwaters came"

Precept Austin notes that Noah and his family had to wait seven days in the ark — "Talk about faith! … God had not told them how long it would be before it began to rain!" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-7-commentary) Enduring Word adds they had never seen rain before (Genesis 2:5), making this "a genuine test of faith, to wait a week after more than 100 years of preparation." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-7/)

Spurgeon, quoted in Precept Austin, imagines the world in its prime when the rain began: "Perhaps the world was in its prime, when the trees were in bloom, and the birds were singing in their branches, and the flowers were blooming on the earth, 'the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up.'" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-7-commentary)

---

### v. 11 — "the six hundredth year … second month, seventeenth day"

**The date.** Ellicott explains this is the civil year beginning in Tisri (autumnal equinox), so the flood began toward the end of October and lasted until spring. The year was a lunar year of 360 days (150 days × 2 = 300, plus adjustments). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/7.htm) The Pulpit Commentary discusses whether "second month" refers to the theocratic year (Nisan, March/April; held by Calvin, Luther, Alford, Wordsworth) or the civil year (Tisri, September/October; held by Josephus, Keil, Murphy, Bush). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm)

**"Fountains of the great deep burst forth."** The NET Bible notes that the same Hebrew term *tehom* ("deep") appears as in Genesis 1:2: "The text seems to picture here subterranean waters coming from under the earth … a judgment involving the reversal of creation." (https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/gen7_notes.htm) Ellicott says this suggests "a great cosmic catastrophe, by which some vast body of water was set loose." Without such a convulsion, he says, it is difficult to understand how the ark could go against the current up to the watershed of Ararat. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/7.htm)

**"Floodgates of the heavens."** The Pulpit Commentary explains *arubboth* (lattice-work, windows): the flood-gates of heaven opened when it rains (cf. Genesis 8:2; 2 Kings 7:19; Malachi 3:10). It notes the language is "metaphorical and optical" but points to a change in land level with ocean waters overflowing, accompanied by heavy rain. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm)

---

### v. 12 — "rain fell … forty days and forty nights"

Precept Austin clarifies that although the rain stopped after forty days, the water level continued to rise for another 110 days and reached its peak after 150 days (Genesis 7:24), with the ark resting on Mount Ararat (Genesis 8:4). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-7-commentary)

---

### vv. 13–15 — "On that very day Noah entered"

**Threefold recital.** The Pulpit Commentary observes that the entry is recorded three times — first in connection with the command (v.5), then in the process during the seven days (v.7), and finally on the day the flood began (v.13) — which "besides lending emphasis to the narrative, heightens its dramatic effect." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm)

**"Every bird of every sort."** Ellicott explains the Hebrew literally says "every bird, every wing," which some understand as three kinds of winged beings: birds generally, singing-birds, and bats/insects. It more probably means "birds of all sorts." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/7.htm)

---

### v. 16 — "the LORD shut him in"

**A deeply significant phrase.** Enduring Word: "Noah did not have to shut the door to keep anyone out of the ark; God alone did it. … It is never the responsibility of God's servants to disqualify people from salvation. If the door is to be shut, God will shut the door." God kept the door open until the last minute, but when it is shut, it is shut — "Jesus is He who opens and no one shuts, and shuts and no one opens (Revelation 3:7)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-7/) The Pulpit Commentary notes the contrast between the divine names: Elohim commands about the beasts, but Jehovah, the covenant God, ensures safety by closing the ark. The LXX renders it "he shut the ark from outside him." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm)

Bible.org (Utley) notes rabbinic tradition that God shut the door to keep the wicked out, "even go so far as to assert that God surrounded the ark with lions and bears to keep the people away." For Utley, this is "another act of YHWH's mercy to mankind to continue the Messianic line … which would eventually provide redemption (cf. Gen. 3:15)." (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-7)

---

### vv. 17–18 — "the waters rose and lifted the ark"

The Pulpit Commentary describes a threefold increase: first, the waters "increased" (the ark floated); second, they "prevailed and increased greatly" (the ark moved); third, they "prevailed exceedingly" (the mountains were submerged). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm) The NET Bible notes that the Hebrew verb *gavar* means "to become great, mighty" — the waters "prevailed" over the earth, overwhelming it. (https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/gen7_notes.htm)

---

### vv. 19–20 — "all the high mountains … covered … to a depth of fifteen cubits"

**Global vs. local flood.** This is the key exegetical divide.

*The global flood view (traditional Protestant):* Enduring Word argues the description "is so complete and specific that it is impossible to reconcile a mere local flood with the Biblical record." It cites over 200 cultures with flood legends (88% describe a favored family, 70% a boat, 95% a flood as sole cause, 67% animals saved, 57% survivors on a mountain). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-7/) The Pulpit Commentary calls it "a clear assertion of the universality of the Flood" (Keil, Kalisch, Alford, Bush, Wordsworth). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm) The Haydock Catholic Commentary: "What part of the world could have been secure, when the waters prevailed fifteen cubits above the highest mountains?" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/genesis/7.htm)

*The local/limited flood view:* Ellicott says the language describes what was within the observer's horizon, not the entire globe: "Far and wide, in every direction, to the utmost reach of the beholder's gaze, no mountain was in sight. … There is no idea here of the mountains of Auvergne." He interprets "the whole heaven" as "the whole horizon." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/7.htm) The Pulpit Commentary acknowledges that "the language does not necessarily imply more than that all the high hills beneath the spectator's heaven were submerged," citing many biblical instances where "all" and "every" have limited signification (Genesis 41:57; Exodus 9:25; Deuteronomy 2:25; 1 Kings 10:24; Acts 2:5; Colossians 1:25). It notes that many "competent scholars" hold the "necessities of exegesis only demand a partial inundation" (Peele, Murphy, Taylor Lewis, 'Speaker's Commentary,' Inglis). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm)

*The Catholic position:* The Catholic Encyclopedia (newadvent.org) carefully distinguishes. It states that "the geographical universality of the Deluge may be safely abandoned" — neither Scripture, tradition, nor science requires it. The Hebrew word translated "earth" (*eretz*) primarily means "land." However, "the Deluge must have been anthropologically universal, i.e. it must have destroyed the whole human race." This is supported by 1 Peter 3:20, 2 Peter 2:4–9, and 2 Peter 3:5ff, which speak of only eight persons saved. (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/04702a.htm)

**"Fifteen cubits."** The NET Bible notes: a cubit is about 18 inches, making 15 cubits about 22.5 feet. The note adds: "Obviously, a flood of twenty feet did not cover the mountains; the statement must mean the flood rose about twenty feet above the highest mountain." (https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/gen7_notes.htm) Ellicott suggests this was the draught (draft/depth) of the ark, computed after it settled near Ararat. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/7.htm)

---

### vv. 21–23 — "every living thing … perished"

**"The breath of life."** Enduring Word makes the point that fish did not drown — only animals on dry land died, "all in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life." It recounts the Scopes Monkey Trial (1925), where Clarence Darrow asked William Jennings Bryan how the fish drowned in the flood: "If he had remembered what the Bible says here, he could have explained … the fish did not die in the flood; only animals with the breath of life in them died." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-7/)

**Noah "only … remained."** The Pulpit Commentary: "The straits to which the advocates of the documentary hypothesis are sometimes reduced are remarkably exemplified by the fortunes of these verses (21–23)." It lists how different critics assign the verses to different sources (Astruc, Eichhorn, Ilgen, Bleek, Davidson) — all contradicting each other. "Amid such uncertainty it will be reasonable to cling to the belief that Moses wrote all the three verses." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm)

---

### v. 24 — "the waters prevailed upon the earth for 150 days"

**Inclusive or additional?** The Pulpit Commentary notes the 150 days may be "additional to the forty days of rain (Murphy), making 190 since the commencement of the Flood; or more probably inclusive of the forty days (Knobel, Lange, Bush, Wordsworth, 'Speaker's Comment.,' Inglis), which, reckoning thirty days to the month, would bring the landing of the ark to the seventeenth day of the seventh month, as stated in Genesis 8:4." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm) Enduring Word adds that "some suggest that God put some or many of the animals on the ark in hibernation for this period, meaning that less food, space, and supervision was necessary." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-7/)

**Spurgeon's typological reading:** "Noah underwent burial to all the old things that he might come out into a new world, and even so we die in Christ that we may live with him." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-7/)

---

## Denominational Distinctives

**Reformed / Calvinist.** The Pulpit Commentary and Spurgeon (both in the Reformed orbit) emphasize divine sovereignty: God shuts the door (v.16), God preserves the remnant, and Noah's righteousness is a matter of justification — being declared righteous — not mere moral goodness. The Pulpit Commentary explicitly links "righteous before me" to the doctrine of justification (Psalm 143:2). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/7.htm) Precept Austin (evangelical with Reformed leanings) stresses that Noah was declared righteous "by grace through faith," citing Hebrews 11:7. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-7-commentary)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic.** Enduring Word (David Guzik) holds a strongly literal, global-flood position and emphasizes practical application — spiritual warfare, testing of faith, and the typology of the ark as Christ. It also cites the worldwide flood legends as apologetic evidence. Guzik applies v.16 pastorally: the servant does not shut the door; only God does. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-7/)

**Catholic.** The Catholic Encyclopedia (newadvent.org) takes a nuanced position: the flood was anthropologically universal (all humans died) but may not have been geographically global. The ark is a type of the Church and of baptism (1 Peter 3:20–21). The Haydock commentary defends a global flood more strongly. (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/04702a.htm) (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/genesis/7.htm)

**Lutheran.** (Not directly found in the searched material. The Lutheran sites lcms.org and 1517.org did not appear in search results for Genesis 7 commentary specifically.)

**Baptist.** Spurgeon (Reformed Baptist, quoted throughout Precept Austin and Enduring Word) emphasizes the gospel call in "Come," the divine power in gathering the animals, and the ark as a picture of Christ. The "shut in" theme is central: God alone closes the door of salvation. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-7-commentary)

**Methodist / Wesleyan.** (Not directly found. The sites seedbed.com and wesley.nnu.edu did not appear in the search results for Genesis 7 specific commentary.)

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes).** The NET Bible notes highlight the "reversal of creation" theme: the same Hebrew word *tehom* ("deep") from Genesis 1:2 reappears in v.11 — God is returning the world to its pre-creation watery state as judgment. The notes also flag the Hebrew idiom "seven seven" (seven pairs or seven individuals) and the prescientific cosmology behind "windows of heaven." (https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/gen7_notes.htm)

**Catholic / Orthodox.** Beyond the Catholic Encyclopedia noted above, the Orthodox Church of America (oca.org) did not appear in search results for Genesis 7-specific material. The Catholic Haydock Commentary (19th century) defends the global flood and insists on a miraculous, not merely natural, cause: "as waters covered the earth at first, so they surely might again, by the power of God." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/genesis/7.htm)

**Anglican (Ellicott).** Ellicott takes a mediating position: he allows for a limited geographic flood (mountains within the observer's horizon), yet insists on the historicity of the event while noting possible use of multiple source documents. He argues that the "120 years" spent building the ark rests on an "untenable interpretation of Genesis 6:3." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/7.htm)

---

*Note: I was unable to retrieve full commentaries from Gill (studyLight), bible.org's full article, Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist (seedbed.com), or Orthodox (oca.org) sources due to tool limitations. The denominational coverage above is therefore partial.*
